overview.text: Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He took office after Franklin D. Roosevelt died, just 82 days after Truman became vice president. A Missouri farmer and World War I artillery officer before entering politics, Truman gained national attention in the Senate for investigating waste in the wartime defense program. His presidency spanned the end of World War II and the early Cold War; his administration supported the Marshall Plan to help rebuild Western Europe. In 1948, despite expectations of defeat and a split in his party over civil rights, Truman won reelection after an energetic campaign.

key_facts.text: Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, on May 8, 1884, and worked as a farmer before his political career.
As a U.S. senator, he chaired an investigation into waste and fraud in the wartime defense program, helping make him a national figure.
Truman became president on April 12, 1945, after Roosevelt’s death; he had become vice president only 82 days earlier.
The Marshall Plan, proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in 1947, led to U.S. funding for Western Europe’s postwar rebuilding.
Truman issued executive orders to desegregate the armed forces and prohibit racial discrimination in federal employment.
He won the 1948 election despite predictions of defeat and a breakaway faction of Southern Democrats opposed to his civil-rights position.
